question: A team sets temperature 0 'so the agent stops making mistakes'. What does temperature 0 actually guarantee?
options: The model only outputs answers it has seen verbatim in its training data
The model refuses to answer whenever its confidence is below a safe threshold
Factual errors are removed because random sampling is the cause of hallucinations
Same input, same most-likely output every time - right or wrong
explanation: Temperature 0 is argmax decoding: deterministic, not correct. If the most likely continuation is wrong, it is wrong every time.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 23

question: A model assigns 0.97 probability to its answer token. What does that number tell you on its own?
options: That the answer is correct about 97 times out of 100 for questions like this one
That 97 % of the training documents contained this exact answer
Its likelihood under the model, which is not the same as being correct
That the answer passed the model's internal fact-checking stage
explanation: Token probabilities describe text continuation; calibration against correctness has to be measured on labelled cases (lesson 24).
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 23

question: Which tokens can top-p (nucleus) sampling never remove from the candidate set?
options: Tokens that are factually incorrect for the specific question the user asked
The most probable ones, even when the most probable token is wrong
Tokens that would make the output invalid JSON
Tokens that repeat something already generated
explanation: Top-p keeps the smallest high-probability prefix; it filters by probability, not by correctness, validity or repetition.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 23

question: An attention head puts most weight on the word 'refund' when the agent chooses the refund tool. What can you conclude?
options: The model chose the tool because of the word 'refund', so removing it will change the choice
Only where that head read from - not why the model chose the tool
All other heads and layers ignored the rest of the input
The tool choice was decided in this layer and later layers only copied it
explanation: Many heads and layers combine; attention weights show where information was read, not a causal explanation.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 23

question: Model B has lower perplexity than model A on a held-out text. What follows for your ticket-triage agent?
options: B predicts that text better; triage quality must still be measured on the task
B will triage more tickets correctly, because perplexity measures overall model quality
B is safer, because lower perplexity means fewer hallucinated facts
B needs less context, because perplexity is measured per token
explanation: Perplexity is intrinsic and comparable only with the same tokenizer and test set; task success needs an extrinsic evaluation.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 23

targets.misconception: Lower perplexity means a better agent

question: An eval report says: pass rate 88 %, 95 % CI [80 %, 94 %]. Which statement is justified?
options: There is a 95 % probability that the agent's true pass rate lies somewhere between 80 % and 94 %
95 % of future evaluations will report a pass rate between 80 % and 94 %
The agent passes between 80 % and 94 % of cases 95 % of the time
Intervals built this way contain the true rate in about 95 % of repeated evaluations
explanation: Coverage is a property of the procedure; any single computed interval either contains the true rate or does not.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 24

targets.misconception: A confidence interval is a probability about one interval

question: You run each of 20 golden cases 10 times (temperature 0.7) and get 200 results. What do you have?
options: A 200-case evaluation with ten times the statistical power of the original
A 200-case evaluation, but only if the seed differs on every run
Repeated measurements of 20 cases, not 200 independent cases
A suite that now covers ten times more of the task's input space
explanation: Independence across task inputs is what makes n; repeats measure model randomness on the same inputs.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 24

targets.misconception: Re-running the same cases adds cases

question: Version A's 95 % interval overlaps version B's. Both ran on the same cases. What should you do next?
options: Conclude there is no difference, because the intervals overlap
Conclude B is worse if its point estimate is lower
Test the paired difference using the cases where exactly one version passed
Run a significance test that treats the two versions' results as independent samples
explanation: Overlap is not a test; paired data call for a paired test (McNemar) on the discordant cases.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 24

question: A regression test reports p = 0.01. Which reading is correct?
options: There is a 99 % probability that the regression is real
With no regression, results this extreme would occur about 1 % of the time
There is a 1 % probability that the new version is better
The regression reduces the pass rate by about 1 percentage point compared with the baseline
explanation: A p-value is computed assuming no effect; it is not the probability that the effect exists, nor its size.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 24

targets.misconception: A p-value is the probability the effect is real

question: An API call fails. When is retrying the same request a bad idea, even though retries are cheap?
options: When the failure will repeat (a 4xx, the same bad input), so another try cannot succeed
Never; with enough retries every request eventually succeeds
Only when the API charges per call, because otherwise a failed retry costs nothing at all
Only when the user is waiting for the answer
explanation: Retry pays only while p_i * C_fail >= c; correlated failures make p_i near 0, and a stuck loop needs a budget.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 25

question: A model writes a 6-step plan for a task. What do you know about it without further checks?
options: It is the cheapest plan the model could find, because models search before answering
It is valid, because the model only proposes steps that exist as tools
It is complete, because planning prompts force the model to list every step
It is one proposal; neither its cost nor its validity is guaranteed until checked or searched
explanation: Search with an admissible heuristic has optimality guarantees; a sampled plan has none and must be verified in code.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 25

targets.misconception: An LLM plan is an optimal plan

question: Can a sufficiently advanced analyser decide, for every script an agent writes, whether it will ever delete data?
options: Yes, given enough compute time and a large enough model
Yes, if the scripts are written in a typed language
Only for scripts shorter than a few hundred lines
No; that would solve the halting problem, so restrict what scripts can call instead
explanation: Rice's theorem: non-trivial behavioural properties are undecidable; allow-lists decide a syntactic property exactly.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 25

targets.misconception: A good analyser can predict any script's behaviour

question: A company adds a reviewer who approves every agent refund before payment. What is the main remaining risk?
options: None; human review removes the agent's errors by definition
The reviewer will reject too many correct refunds because people distrust AI
The reviewer may come to approve by default because the agent is usually right (automation bias)
Legal liability moves from the company to the reviewer
explanation: Oversight works only if reviewers can and do disagree; measure catch rates (AI Act Art. 14(4)(b); Parasuraman & Riley).
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 26

targets.misconception: A human in the loop makes it safe

question: A chatbot answer ends with 'Check our policy page for details'. The answer misstates the policy and a customer relies on it. Who is likely responsible?
options: The customer, because the disclaimer told them to check the policy page
The company deploying the chatbot, as for any other statement on its website
The model vendor, because the model generated the wrong statement
Nobody, because chatbot output is not a statement by the company
explanation: Moffatt v. Air Canada: the chatbot is part of the company's website and the company is responsible for its information.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 26

question: An agent runs on a local model on the office Mac mini. Which statement about personal data is correct?
options: Data protection still applies to prompts, memories, logs and backups that contain personal data
Data protection does not apply because no data leaves the building
Only the model weights need protection, because they encode the training data
Personal data may be kept indefinitely because local storage is cheap
explanation: Local hosting reduces transfer risk but not duties such as minimisation, retention and rights over automated decisions.
source: Concept inventory (pre/post); misconception addressed in Lesson 26
